pages.title: Good or Bad UX
pages.content:
**“The overall experience of a person using a product such as a website or computer application, especially in terms of how easy or pleasing it is to use.”**

That right there… is the dictionary definition of “User Experience” Design for digital products. In short, UX design. 

There is no wonder that every product around you is designed. There is no such thing as “No Design”. They are either well designed or ill designed. 

Have you ever walked up to a door tried to pull it with the handle when all it needed was a gentle push to open? The Norman Door, named after design extraordinaire Don Norman, is any door that is confusing to use.

pages.title: User is the King
pages.content:
As a Developer of digital products, such as websites and applications, it becomes our responsibility to ensure that the products we design entail a good experience for its users.

The competition on the online is just one tab away. We must ensure our products sustain for a longer time and the users keep using our website for their needs.

The step one of designing user friendly web interfaces is to **understand where our users are coming from and what are their primary goals on a given interface**. 
Once we understand the user context, we can then take better interface level decisions as to how we want the UI elements to be situated on the interface.

pages.title: Process of building a software
pages.content:
The key to developing a user-friendly digital product is to **involve users in the design process by taking their feedback**.\
There are many user centric frameworks that help designers to come up with solutions to wicked problems, such as the double diamond, design thinking etc. 

However, in this course, as developers, understanding the following **User Centric Software Development Cycle** will help you become more empathetic towards the process. Moreover, it is a more practical approach implemented by many fast paced teams.

The heart of this cycle are the **three iterative cycles** that exist at three different stages of the life cycle as annotated 1,2 and 3.

pages.title: The team
pages.content:
Now that we spoke about an ideal User Centric Software Development Cycle, let us talk about how you can fit in the process better and what role you shall play in the whole process. 

Ideally, the team will comprise **a Product Manager**, who will overlook the whole process, prioritise the tasks, and manage the timeline. 

**A designer or more**, depending on the scope of the project. Some projects might demand User researchers, Usability Experts, Visual and UI designers separately. 

And finally **Engineers and Developers** like you and me!

pages.title: Tracking patterns
pages.content:
You are now aware what it takes to build User Friendly web products. 

**1. A user centric process that takes User Feedbacks and multiple iterations. \
2. A cross functioning team of experts.**

Now, let us slowly move into what constitutes in a web Product with good UX. \
Let us start with **"tracking"**.


**Fun fact! 60% of visitors spend less than 15 seconds** trying to orient on the web. \
It is thus important when we arrange the content on our website, we place the most crucial and sought after information at the focal points where users will be more likely to pay attention.

constraints:
- $1 \leq T \leq 100$
- $1 \leq N \leq 100$
- $1 \leq M \leq N\cdot(N-1)/2$
- $1 \leq u_i, v_i \leq N$
- $u_i \neq v_i$ for each $1 \leq i \leq M$.
- The sum of $N$ over all test cases won't exceed $100$.
practiceProblems.inputFormat:
- The first line of input will contain a single integer $T$, denoting the number of test cases.
- Each test case consists of multiple lines of input.

practiceProblems.outputFormat: For each test case, output on a new line the number of good subgraphs of $G$, modulo $10^9 + 7$.

pages.title: Grouping, Proximity and Common Region
pages.content:
**The Laws of Proximity and Common Region** are often used in interface design.

It explains how people decide whether an **element** is a part of a group and are especially helpful for interface designers because they help set up a hierarchy by putting elements into groups.

Let's look at the application of each of these laws in web design!

pages.title: Common region
pages.content:
**The principle of common region says that items within a boundary are perceived as a group and assumed to share some common characteristic or functionality.**

The laws of Proximity and Common region are two of the 7 Gestalt Principles that guides interface designers to arrange elements on the interface to make it easier for users to make sense of the information.

pages.title: Padding and Margin
pages.content:
As we discuss the various aspects of spacing, let us explore the two key spacing terms. **Padding and Margins**

**Padding** is the spacing between elements and the related content inside it.
It determines how elements look and sit within a container. 

**Margin** is the space around an element. Margins are used to move an element up or down on a page as well as left or right.

pages.title: Typography
pages.content:
Perhaps no single topic is more underrated in website design than **typography**. 

Typography determines how text looks to the reader, how the words literally appear on a page or screen.\
On top of ease-of-reading, digital text must be designed for:
1. Shorter attention spans 
2. Skimmability
3. Accessibility
4. Multiple device types and screen sizes
